name: Castillo San Felipe del Morro
label: El Morro
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Paseo del Morro' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Paseo del Morro nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/561634537: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castillo San Felipe del Morro' (273 m across).
notes: The famous 16th-century Spanish fortress at the tip of Old San Juan.

text.description:
El Morro is the great stone fortress at the north-western tip of Old San Juan, standing on a steep headland where the Atlantic meets the entrance to San Juan Bay. Building began in 1539 as a fortified tower, and by 1595 it had grown into a larger bastion fort. Work carried on for roughly two more centuries, and it reached its present form in 1787. The walls rise about 43 metres from the shoreline and are several metres thick, which is why the fort looks so solid in a photo. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1983.

It photographs well because the fort, the sea wall, the surf and the green slope can all sit in one frame. From here the fort is just to the east, close up and seen from the water side. Guides describe it as quieter than the main lawn, with clean backgrounds and good light towards sunset. The walkway can be reached on foot from the Paseo de la Princesa end. If you want a second view, the lawn in front of the fort shows the stone facade and lighthouse above the grass, with the horizon behind. Plaza del Quinto Centenario gives a higher angle back towards the castle from the city side.
text.geographic_location: In the Old San Juan historic quarter, on the north-western point of the old city's islet, where the headland guards the entrance to San Juan Bay. The Paseo del Morro walkway runs along the sea wall below the fort.
text.directions_text: Head for Old San Juan and make for the Paseo del Morro. If you are already walking the waterfront, the free approach is from the Paseo de la Princesa end, following the sea wall towards the fort. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the fort. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the wall, surf and green slope into one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the lighthouse or the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Paseo del Morro (the paved walkway that runs along the sea wall from the Raíces side up to the fort). The fort seen close up from the water side, with the wall, the surf and the lush slope in one frame. The fort is to the east of you. From here you see it close up from the water side, with the wall, the surf and the lush slope together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the sea wall along a lower line so the fort rises above it. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, try the lawn in front of the fort, which shows the facade and lighthouse above the grass, or Plaza del Quinto Centenario for a higher angle looking back at the castle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fort's stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Take a few Live Photos or short bursts where the surf hits the wall, then pick the best frame. Wipe your lens first, as sea air can leave a film on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, according to several guides, when the walkway and lawn are the best places to be.

text.access_note: The Paseo del Morro walkway is reported to be free to walk from the Paseo de la Princesa end. One visitor review says entering the Paseo from the fort side carries a fee. The fort's interior and ramparts close in the late afternoon, so check the official site for current access before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Sea spray and humid sea air can leave a film on a phone lens, so wiping it before shooting helps.
Dragging the exposure slider down slightly helps keep sky colour in a bright scene.

name: La Fortaleza
label: La Fortaleza
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Fortaleza' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Calle de la Fortaleza' (way/60330126): point nearest the subject (331 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3501975: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'La Fortaleza' (82 m across).
notes: The governor's palace, one of the oldest executive mansions in the Americas.

text.description:
La Fortaleza, also called the Palacio de Santa Catalina, is the official residence and workplace of the Governor of Puerto Rico. It stands in the western part of Old San Juan. Building began in 1533 as a fortress and finished in 1540. It was remodelled in 1846 into the Neoclassical palace you see today. It has housed the governor since the 16th century, which makes it the oldest executive mansion in continuous use in the Americas. It was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1983.

For a phone photo, the best approach is along Calle Fortaleza. The street is closed to traffic and rises toward the palace, with colonial facades on both sides and the building as the focal point at the top. Overhead decorations such as umbrellas, kites or a flag are sometimes hung above the street, and they change over time, so check what is up when you arrive. The palace exterior has been painted in white, light blue and light grey, which gives a soft, clean backdrop to the busier colours of the street.

If you want a different view, Plazuela de Rogativa sits beside the fortress and looks over San Juan Bay. It is a good option for sunset, but check the angle on arrival. The exterior and surrounding streets are free to photograph. Going inside is possible only on a guided tour.
text.geographic_location: La Fortaleza is in the western part of Old San Juan, the historic quarter on San Juan Islet, close to the walls that face San Juan Bay. Calle Fortaleza leads up to it.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so plan your own way to Old San Juan. Walk west, uphill, toward the palace, which is about 430 m on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole street and the palace at the top. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the facades and any overhead decoration. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the palace at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Fortaleza (Stand at the lower end and face uphill toward the governor's residence). The car-free street rising toward La Fortaleza, framed by colonial facades and whatever overhead decoration is hung that season (umbrellas, kites, or a flag). From here you see the car-free street rising between colonial facades, with the palace closing the view at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the palace at the end of the street and let the facades make leading lines on both sides. Switch on gridlines and keep the verticals straight. If something is hung across the street, such as umbrellas, kites or a flag, include it at the top of the frame. For a different view, try Plazuela de Rogativa, which looks at the fortress from a raised, quieter angle with the bay behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the pale walls keep their detail. If people walk through the frame, take a short burst or a Live Photo and pick the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people. Plazuela de Rogativa is a good option at sunset.

text.access_note: The street and the outside of the building are free to photograph, but the inside of La Fortaleza is reachable only on guided tours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit more of the facades and overhead decoration into a fairly narrow street.
People walking through the street may spoil a frame, so a short burst or a Live Photo can help you catch a clear moment.
Lowering the exposure slider slightly helps keep detail in the sky and the pale walls.

name: Isla Verde Beach
label: Isla Verde Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Playa Isla Verde' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Isla Verde, Puerto Rico' (found by searching for the spot's name).
notes: Popular wide beach beside the airport and the hotels.

text.description: Isla Verde Beach is the long stretch of sand in front of one of the main tourist and resort areas of the San Juan metropolitan area. The name means "green island" in Spanish, after a small cay and reef a little way off the shore. The district is packed with hotels and condominiums, so you get a wide curve of golden sand and turquoise water with a skyline of buildings behind it. The beach also sits right next to Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport, so planes come in low over the water on their final approach. That means a passing aircraft can be your subject. Isla Verde is officially part of the municipality of Carolina, although it shares its coastline with Ocean Park and Condado, which are part of San Juan. For photos, stand on the sand near the waterline and decide first whether you want the planes or the beach and hotels. For the planes, wait for one to appear and keep plenty of sky above the sand. For the beach itself, keep the waves in the foreground and the hotel line on the far side. Parking nearby is reported to be difficult, so plan how you will arrive.
text.geographic_location: Isla Verde lies on the Atlantic coast east of Ocean Park and Condado, between the San Juan side of the metropolitan area and Piñones. It is technically in the municipality of Carolina, and the airport sits just to its south.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so start from Condado or Old San Juan and go east by taxi, or by AMA bus 5 or 53 to the Isla Verde bus terminal (about 1 hour from Old San Juan). Isla Verde is roughly 3 to 6 miles (4.8 to 9.7 km) east of those areas. Parking is reported to be difficult, so a taxi is the easier choice. Once on the beach, the subject is about 5 minutes on foot north of the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 320 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long beach and the hotel skyline, and the default lens (1x) for a planes-over-the-sand view. If your phone has telephoto/zoom (2x-5x), it brings an approaching aircraft closer, but keep some sky around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 320 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Stand on Playa Isla Verde, on the sand facing northeast toward the airport approach path, with the sea and the beach in front of you. From the shoreline you can frame low aircraft on final approach to Luis Muñoz Marín Airport against the sky above the beach.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower line, leaving two thirds of the frame for sky, so a plane has room to cross it. Tap on the plane or the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the aircraft stays crisp and the sky keeps its colour. For a different view, shoot along the sand with the ultra-wide (0.5x), keeping the turquoise water in the foreground and the hotels on the far side. Balneario del Escambrón is an alternative viewpoint from further along the coast, showing the Condado/Ocean Park and Isla Verde waterfront from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Take several shots as each plane passes, because the moment goes quickly. Check your first photo and adjust the exposure slider if the sky is washed out or the aircraft looks too dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon is best for the planes over the beach. For the beach and hotel skyline lit by early sunlight, go in the early morning.

text.access_note: The beach is open shoreline, but access routes, parking and hotel areas may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Condado Beach
label: Condado Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida Ashford' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Avenida Dr. Ashford' (roads).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q49320432: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Beachfront and the Ventana al Mar sunset viewpoint.

text.description: Condado Beach is a large public beach on the Atlantic side of San Juan, in the Condado district of Santurce, just east of the old islet. It runs from La Ventana al Mar Park on Ashford Avenue in the west to Punta Piedrita in the east. Behind it stands a row of well-known hotels, including La Concha Resort, the San Juan Marriott and the historic Vanderbilt Hotel. That mix of open sand and hotel frontage is why it photographs well. The classic picture is taken along Avenida Ashford, where the beachfront hotel strip meets the sand. Crouch low on the sand so the golden foreground fills the bottom of the frame and the mid-century hotel facades line up behind it. Golden hour is the best moment for this view. If you want a different angle, Puente Dos Hermanos gives a sweeping bridge shot with the Atlantic, the Condado Lagoon and the San Juan skyline behind it. Playa del Condado gives a closer, quieter frame of sand and surf. Take care near the water. The waves can be stronger than they look, and winter swells (December to March) are larger, so keep your phone and your feet back from the shoreline. Check conditions before you stand close to the surf.
text.geographic_location: Condado Beach is in the Condado district of Santurce, on San Juan's Atlantic coast, directly east of the Islet of San Juan. It sits along Ashford Avenue, backed by the beachfront hotels.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Condado, the district just east of the Islet of San Juan. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sand and the long line of hotels. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the facades. If you want a tighter shot of one hotel or the bridge, try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from a safe distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenida Ashford (stretch of the beachfront hotel strip, shot from the sand at low angle). Golden sand in the foreground with the mid-century hotel facades lining the beach behind it. From the sand there, the view shows golden sand in the foreground and the mid-century hotel facades lining the beach behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch or hold the phone low, close to the sand, so the foreground fills the bottom of the frame and the hotels sit behind. Turn on the gridlines and keep the line of facades level. For a different view, try Puente Dos Hermanos, where the bridge sweeps across the frame with the lagoon and skyline behind it. Playa del Condado gives a closer, quieter frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the facades to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sand does not turn white. Wipe the lens first, as sea spray leaves a haze on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, shooting from a low angle.

text.access_note: Condado Beach is a public-access beach, but check that the beachfront stretch of Avenida Ashford is open to pedestrians when you visit, and check the official site before you go if you are unsure.

name: Castillo San Cristóbal
label: San Cristóbal Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Garita del Diablo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'La Garita del Diablo' (way/561590374): middle (44 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W142863669 (Castillo San Cristóbal): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The largest Spanish fortification in the Americas, guarding the city's east side.

text.description: Castillo San Cristóbal is the big stone fort on the Atlantic side of Old San Juan. For a phone photo, the best subject here is the Garita del Diablo, a small sentry box that juts out over the cliff at the sea's edge. It is the most photographed feature on the ocean side of the fort. It works well because it is a simple, strong shape with nothing behind it but the Atlantic, so there is little clutter to manage. The usual shot is taken from the rampart, looking back at the sentry box, with the sea filling the background. The grounds, ramparts and sentry box are part of a ticketed National Park Service site, so plan to go in rather than shoot from outside. Opening times can vary, so check the official site for current hours and tickets before you go. Start with the default lens (1x) so you can see the whole sentry box against the sea, then step back and try 2x for a tighter, flatter view. Tap the sentry box to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Keep well back from the edge, and keep one hand firmly on the phone. If you want a second picture, the fort also gives a wide view over the rooftops of Old San Juan, the harbour and the Atlantic horizon. Plaza de Colón, which is free, shows the fort as a large stone mass at the end of the streets.
text.geographic_location: Castillo San Cristóbal is in Old San Juan, on the Atlantic-facing side of the old town. The Garita del Diablo shot is described separately: it is taken from the rampart, looking back at the sentry box.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Old San Juan on foot. Once inside the fort, follow the ramparts on the Atlantic side to reach the sentry box. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole sentry box and the sea behind it. Switch to 2x for a tighter shot that takes in less of the wall around it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole rampart and sweep of coast in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (outside the seaward wall, shot from the rampart looking back at the sentry box). The small sentry box jutting out over the cliff at the sea's edge, with the Atlantic filling the background. For the Garita del Diablo shot, stand on the rampart and look back at the sentry box, which sits out over the cliff, outside the seaward wall. The box should fill part of the frame, with the Atlantic filling the background behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the sentry box on one of the thirds, leaving the open sea and sky on the other side. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, the fort also gives a wide panorama over the Old San Juan rooftops and harbour, or you can shoot the fort from Plaza de Colón.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sentry box to lock focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames, because sea wind can make a handheld phone shake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds arrive, gives the best chance of empty ramparts. Check the current opening time on the official site first.

text.access_note: The fort's grounds, ramparts and the Garita del Diablo are inside a ticketed National Park Service site, so check the official site before you go for current hours and entry.

name: Paseo de la Princesa
label: Paseo de la Princesa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fuente Raíces' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fuente de las Raíces' (way/344551844): middle (18 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q49540041: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Tree-lined promenade along the old city wall and the bay.

text.description:
Paseo de la Princesa is a tree-lined pedestrian promenade of about 0.8 km along the southwestern edge of Old San Juan, running beside the old city walls. It was built between 1852 and 1854 and named for Princess Infanta Isabel, the first-born child of Queen Isabella II of Spain. It was restored in 1989. Victorian-style lampposts, benches, gardens and sculptures line the way, and at weekends there is often live music and there are street vendors.

The best-known picture here is Fuente Raíces, the Roots Fountain. This large sculptural fountain by Luis Sanguino dates from 1992 and celebrates the Taino, Spanish and Sub-Saharan African roots of Puerto Rican identity. It works well in a phone photo because the sculpture gives you a strong foreground, while the trees, lampposts and old walls lead the eye back along the promenade. Guides often suggest sunset, when the light on the fountain is at its warmest. A small wooden dock beside the fountain's plaza looks out over San Juan Bay.

On days when cruise ships are in, the promenade gets much busier, especially around midday. Early or late visits give you more space for a clean shot. Stand at the fountain and look back along the paseo toward the walls and the bay. The Puerta de San Juan at the far end is a good second photo.
text.geographic_location: Paseo de la Princesa is in Old San Juan, on the southwestern side of the old city, running alongside the historic walls close to the cruise ship harbour. It ends at the Puerta de San Juan, near La Fortaleza.
text.directions_text: Head for Old San Juan and ask for Paseo de la Princesa; no station or tram stop is listed nearby, and the promenade is close to the cruise ship harbour. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the fountain, the promenade and the walls into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the sculpture figures or the lampposts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (at the far end of the promenade, looking back along the paseo toward the walls and bay). The Raíces fountain in the foreground, with the tree-lined promenade and the historic walls receding behind it. Walk to the Fuente Raíces plaza and take the view from the fountain. Check on the day exactly where the fountain sits along the promenade. From the fountain, the sculpture fills the foreground, with the tree-lined promenade and the historic walls receding behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Face back along the paseo toward the walls and the bay. Keep the fountain low in the frame and let the line of trees and lampposts lead the eye into the distance. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level. If you want a different view, the Puerta de San Juan at the far end shows the old gate with the wall beside it and the bay behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water looks washed out. At sunset, a Live Photo can catch moving people and water. Use night mode only once the light has really faded.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, according to several guides. Cruise-ship days make the promenade much busier, especially midday, so early morning or late afternoon is calmer.

text.access_note: This is a public promenade with no entry requirement, but check the official site before you go for any events or closures.

name: San Juan Gate
label: San Juan Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plazuela de la Rogativa' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plazuela de la Rogativa' (relation/3613992): middle (70 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N2306823907 (San Juan Gate): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Red-painted gate of the old city wall, once the entrance from the harbour.

text.description: San Juan Gate is the red gate set into the old stone city walls, with colonial buildings and the bay close by. The red against the stone makes it an easy subject for a phone, because it stands out even in a quick snap. The best all-round view is from the small plaza uphill from the gate, Plazuela de la Rogativa on Caleta de las Monjas. The statue in the plaza usually sits in the foreground, which gives the picture depth and a sense of place. Take a few frames at different zoom levels: one wide for the whole scene, one closer on the gate and the wall. If you want a second angle, walk down and photograph the gate framed against the stonework, or step outside the walls to see the gate and its sentry box from the Paseo del Morro side, with the path leading away behind it. Keep in mind that this stretch of path is short on the gate side, and you cannot enter El Morro fort from outside the wall. One visitor reported that the walkway out over the beach was closed, so check access before you head that way. Allow only a few minutes here, as the plaza and the gate are very close together.
text.geographic_location: San Juan Gate stands in the old walled part of San Juan, on the line of the city walls near the bay. Plazuela de la Rogativa, the viewing plaza, is on Caleta de las Monjas just uphill from it, close to La Fortaleza.
text.directions_text: Head for the old walled part of San Juan, the nearest well-known area, and walk to Caleta de las Monjas and Plazuela de la Rogativa. Walk about 70 m downhill to the south-east to reach it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate, bay and walls together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the statue large in the foreground, and to 2x telephoto to pick out the red gate from the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plazuela de la Rogativa (small plaza on Caleta de las Monjas, uphill from the gate). A wider view of the gate with the bay, La Fortaleza, and the city walls around it, usually including the statue in the foreground. The small plaza on Caleta de las Monjas, uphill from the gate. From here the photo shows a wider view of the gate with the bay, La Fortaleza and the city walls around it, usually with the statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the gate on one of the lower intersections, with the statue off to one side for depth. Keep the horizon level along the bay. For a different view, try the gate framed against the stone walls, or from outside the walls on the Paseo del Morro side, where the gate and its sentry box sit with the path behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red gate to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the red stays rich and the bright sky does not wash out. Take a Live Photo if people are passing, so you can pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No fixed best time is given. Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the stone and the red paint than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The plaza is a free public square, but check access to the walkways and paths beside the walls before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and kinder to the stone and the red paint than midday sun.
The gate is red and stands out against the stone of the walls (taken from the viewpoint notes; colour described as red).

name: Cathedral of San Juan Bautista
label: San Juan Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle del Cristo' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle del Cristo nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/255583481: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'San Cathedral Basilica of Saint John the Baptist' (83 m across).
notes: Added back after the name lookup fix (2026-11-16).

text.description:
The Cathedral of San Juan Bautista stands in the Old San Juan historic district and is one of the oldest buildings in the Americas. It is the oldest purpose-built cathedral still standing in the Americas. The first church on the site was made of wood from 1513, but a hurricane destroyed it in 1529. A stone building followed between 1535 and 1542. An earthquake in 1787 led to a rebuild in 1802, which gave the cathedral its current Baroque look, and the facade was altered again in 1905 after another earthquake. Inside, you can still see Gothic vaults in the north-east corner. The tomb of Juan Ponce de León is here too.

For a phone photo, the bright white facade is the draw. It looks very good against the colonial street and the colourful buildings around it. The best view is from the stretch of Calle del Cristo in front of the cathedral. Go early if you can. Between about 6:30 and 8:00 a.m. the street is quiet and the light is soft, so you can get a clean shot without strangers in it. Late in the afternoon the shadows can turn harsh. If you go inside, the vaulted nave, the altar area and the stained-glass windows are worth a few frames. Services come first, so be discreet, and ask before photographing people.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in the Old San Juan historic district, on Calle del Cristo.
text.directions_text: The spot is in Old San Juan, on Calle del Cristo. From there the cathedral's centre is about 1 minute on foot to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the facade from the narrow street, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the doorway and upper facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle del Cristo (stretch in front of the cathedral facade). The white Gothic-style facade of the cathedral, framed by the colonial street. From here you see the white front of the cathedral framed by the colonial street, with the cathedral lying to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the facade up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Include a little of the street and the neighbouring buildings to show the colonial setting. If you want a different view, go inside and photograph the vaulted nave, the altar area and the stained-glass windows, with the tomb of Juan Ponce de León.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white stonework keeps its detail instead of turning pale. Hold the phone steady against your body or a wall for sharper shots in the early light.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, about 6:30–8:00 a.m., when the street is empty and the light is soft. Late afternoon can bring harsh shadows.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a place of worship, so dress modestly, keep quiet during services, and check the official site before you go for visiting times and photography rules.

name: Santa María Magdalena de Pazzis Cemetery
label: Old San Juan Cemetery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Castillo San Felipe del Morro' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Castillo San Felipe del Morro' (way/561634537): middle (272 m across); moved 40 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28966510: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cementerio Santa María Magdalena de Pazzis' (340 m across).
notes: White cemetery on the seafront below El Morro.

text.description:
The Santa María Magdalena de Pazzis Cemetery is a historic Catholic cemetery in Old San Juan. It sits right beside the Atlantic, just outside the walls of Castillo San Felipe del Morro. Building began in 1863, and many of Puerto Rico's best-known writers, musicians, politicians and activists are buried here. The site was chosen so that it looks out over the ocean, and the sea view was meant to symbolise the spirit's journey to the afterlife. The wall averages about 12 metres in height.

It photographs well because of the contrast: white tombs and walls against blue water, with the fort's heavy stonework close by. The best overall picture is the overhead view from the grassy field at the fort's exit, looking down towards the cemetery. Walk down the slope after leaving El Morro and you get the whole white cemetery with the sea behind it and the fort's walls beside it.

For a second picture, go down to the cemetery itself. From among the tombs you can see El Morro on one side and La Perla on the other. Keep your voice down and stay on the paths, as this is a working place of remembrance. Take wide scenes first, then move in for details such as carved stone and crosses.
text.geographic_location: In Old San Juan, on the Atlantic-facing edge of the old city, just outside the walls of Castillo San Felipe del Morro. La Perla lies on its other side.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Castillo San Felipe del Morro, then leave the fort and head onto the grassy field at its exit. If you want to go down to the cemetery gate afterwards, follow the slope down towards the white walls. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall view of the cemetery, the sea and the fort walls. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the fort and sky in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the white tombs and the cemetery walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Castillo San Felipe del Morro (grassy field at the fort's exit, looking down toward the cemetery). An overhead view of the white, ocean-side cemetery with the fort's walls nearby. From here you look down on the white, ocean-side cemetery, with the fort's walls close by. The cemetery is to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the cemetery along the lower third, so the sea and sky fill the rest. Include a bit of the fort's wall at the edge of the frame to give a sense of scale. For a different shot, go down to the cemetery itself and photograph the tombs with El Morro on one side and La Perla on the other. The approach along Calle Cementerio, framed by the white walls, is another option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so they keep their detail against the bright sky. Take a 0.5x shot and a 1x shot from the same spot so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white walls than the middle of the day. Check which way the sun falls on the day you visit.

text.access_note: The cemetery is a historic Catholic burial ground, so visit respectfully, and check the official site before you go for El Morro and cemetery visiting rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer on white walls than midday light.
The cemetery is a working place of remembrance where visitors should keep quiet and stay on the paths.
White walls can lose detail against a bright sky unless the exposure is lowered slightly.

name: San José Church
label: San José Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza del Quinto Centenario' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza del Quinto Centenario' (way/196604234): middle (108 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/256388549: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Joseph Catholic Church' (66 m across).
notes: Gothic church from the 1530s on Plaza San José.

text.description:
San José Church is one of the earliest surviving examples of 16th-century Spanish Gothic architecture in the Western Hemisphere. It was begun in 1528 and founded in 1532 as part of a Dominican convent dedicated to Thomas Aquinas. It was built in the Isabelline style, a blend of late Gothic and early Renaissance Spanish architecture. Juan Ponce de León, the first governor of Puerto Rico, was buried in its crypt from 1559 until 1836. A long restoration finished in March 2021, so the building is in good shape for photos.

It photographs well because of its age and setting. The weathered church sits among the narrow streets of Old San Juan, so you get the building and the town around it in one frame. From Plaza del Quinto Centenario you see the church from the side, at a three-quarter angle. That shows the depth of the building and its place among the neighbouring streets, and it is a good change from the straight-on view. For the classic full-façade shot with the bell-tower side, walk on to Plaza de San José and shoot across the open plaza.

The church is close to the plaza, so you can take both views in a few minutes. The outside views from the plazas do not depend on the church being open, but the doors have sometimes been found closed, so check opening hours before planning to go in.
text.geographic_location: San José Church is in Old San Juan, the historic colonial quarter of the city. It stands close to Plaza del Quinto Centenario and the Museo de las Américas.
text.directions_text: Head for Plaza del Quinto Centenario in Old San Juan. For the full-façade view, continue on to Plaza de San José. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the three-quarter view of the church. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the streets feel tight and you cannot fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the doorway and the upper part of the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza del Quinto Centenario. A side or three-quarter view of the church from the nearby plaza, with the building set among the surrounding Old San Juan streets. From here you see a side or three-quarter view of the church, set among the surrounding Old San Juan streets. The church is to the south-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the church along one of the vertical lines, so the walls do not lean. Keep a little of the street or plaza in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a second angle, walk to Plaza de San José and take the straight-on view of the façade and bell-tower side across the open plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, or brace it against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: Visitors have sometimes found the church doors closed, so check opening hours before going in; the views from the plazas do not depend on it being open.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows than midday.
The streets of Old San Juan are narrow, so the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can help fit the whole building in.
Keeping the gridlines on helps keep the vertical walls straight in the photo.

name: Calle del Cristo and Christ Chapel
label: Capilla del Cristo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque de las Palomas' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque de las Palomas' (way/196604231): middle (82 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/268171786: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Capilla del Santo Cristo de la Salud' (15 m across).
notes: Tiny chapel at the end of the cobbled Calle del Cristo.

text.description:
Capilla del Cristo is a small stone chapel at the foot of Calle del Cristo, a pedestrian street in Old San Juan, close to La Fortaleza. It was built in the 18th century in the Spanish Baroque style, and most of the objects on its altar date from 1753. A curved belfry sits on top, and three wide arches open towards Parque de las Palomas, Tetuán Street and Calle de Cristo de la Salud. Its gate was added in the 1940s to protect the interior, and a volunteer brotherhood still looks after the building.

It photographs well because the chapel is so compact. The white bell tower and arches make a clear subject, and from the little park beside it you can set them against the bay and harbour on the other side of the city wall. The chapel's front is a popular image on Puerto Rican travel guides and souvenirs, so you will recognise the view when you see it.

For a phone, the park is the easier spot. It is usually calmer than the street, and the harbour behind the chapel adds depth. If you want the classic straight-on view with the cobbled street leading to the chapel, take that as a second shot from the upper end of Calle del Cristo, looking back down towards the chapel (a suggested position, not a confirmed spot). The chapel is reportedly open only on certain days, so treat the interior as a bonus, and plan around the outside.
text.geographic_location: In the Old San Juan Historic District, at the foot of Calle del Cristo beside Parque de las Palomas and the city wall, not far from La Fortaleza.
text.directions_text: No station, tram stop or other public transport is listed for this spot. Head for the Old San Juan Historic District, near La Fortaleza. Walk to the bottom of Calle del Cristo, where the chapel stands, and step into the small Parque de las Palomas beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the chapel, bell tower and harbour together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the arches and the wall in a tight space, and use telephoto (2x or more) for the belfry on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque de las Palomas (beside the chapel, on the city wall overlooking the harbor). The chapel and its bell tower framed against the bay and harbor from the small park beside it. The small park beside the chapel on the city wall overlooking the harbour. From here the chapel and its bell tower sit against the bay and harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bell tower on one of the vertical lines, leaving the harbour in the rest of the frame. Keep the phone level so the chapel walls don't lean. For a second picture, you could walk up to the upper end of Calle del Cristo and shoot back down the street, with the cobbled road and colourful colonial facades leading to the chapel. Treat this as a suggested position, not a confirmed spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white chapel wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and water keep their colour and the stone doesn't burn out. Take a few frames, as people often walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is calmer, as the street is reportedly busy by late morning. Some guides suggest the park for sunset.

text.access_note: The park and street are outdoors and open to walk around; the chapel itself is reportedly open only on certain days, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The street is reportedly busy by late morning, so earlier visits are calmer.
Some guides suggest Parque de las Palomas as a sunset viewpoint.
Parque de las Palomas is usually less crowded than Calle del Cristo.
The upper end of Calle del Cristo, looking back down towards the chapel, is a suggested second viewpoint (an inference, not a confirmed spot).

name: Puerto Rico Capitol
label: El Capitolio
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza San Juan Bautista' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'San Juan Bautista' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/59744985: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Puerto Rico Capitol' (133 m across).
notes: White marble capitol building on the Puerta de Tierra.

text.description: The Capitol of Puerto Rico, El Capitolio, is the seat of the island's Legislative Assembly. It stands just outside the walls of Old San Juan, in Puerta de Tierra. The building is clad in white marble and was built between 1921 and 1929 in a Neoclassical Beaux-Arts style. Architect Rafael Carmoega designed it to resemble the Pantheon in Rome. It has been on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places since 1977. Its main façade faces the Atlantic Ocean, which is why it photographs so well: white steps and columns with open sea and sky behind. The building is wide, so start with the full frontage and then move in for details such as the columns and the dome. Keep the phone level, because the straight lines of the steps and columns look best when the horizon is not tilted. If you want a different angle, the sea-facing front is the classic one, and you can also try the dome from Paseo de la Princesa.
text.geographic_location: In Puerta de Tierra, on San Juan Islet, immediately outside the city walls of Old San Juan. The Capitol sits on high ground between the Atlantic Ocean to the north and San Juan Bay to the south.
text.directions_text: From Old San Juan, head east to Puerta de Tierra and look for El Capitolio. The Capitol is roughly 1.6 km (about 1 mile) in a straight line from La Fortaleza at the western end of the islet. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the frontal view of the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the full width in, and use telephoto (2x or more) for the columns and dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza San Juan Bautista (north side of the Capitol, facing the Atlantic). The Capitol's main north façade and white marble steps with the ocean behind, the classic frontal postcard view. On Plaza San Juan Bautista, on the north side of the Capitol, facing the Atlantic. This is the classic frontal postcard view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the portico with the middle of the screen so the building looks balanced. Keep the horizon level and let some sea and sky show above and beside the building. For a different angle, the white dome framed by palm trees from Paseo de la Princesa works well, and Playa del Capitolio gives a quieter shoreline view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the white stone keeps its detail and does not turn pale. Ultra-wide shots can bend the edges of the building, so keep the Capitol in the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the white marble. Check which way the sun falls on the day, because the front faces north.

text.access_note: The exterior and Plaza San Juan Bautista can be photographed from outside, but the interior may close during legislative sessions or construction and tour access can be limited, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light on the white marble than midday.
Because the main façade faces north, direct sun on the front is limited for much of the day, so check the light on the day.
White marble can lose detail in bright light on a phone, so lowering the exposure slider helps.

name: Casa Blanca
label: Casa Blanca
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Paseo del Morro' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Paseo del Morro nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/269739384: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Casa Blanca' (47 m across).
notes: Ponce de León family's 16th-century house with a garden.

text.description:
Casa Blanca is a white, fortified house on a rise above San Juan Bay, in Old San Juan. Building began in 1521, and it was meant to be the home of Juan Ponce de León and his family. He died on an expedition to Florida without ever living there. It later became the first governor's residence in Puerto Rico, and it was built with solid walls and terraces for guards and artillery. Today it is a house museum run by the Institute of Puerto Rican Culture, with 16th- and 17th-century objects inside and a garden with fountains.

It photographs well because the pale walls stand out against the bay and the old city wall beside it. The most useful picture is the wide one from Paseo del Morro, where you can fit the whole southwest facade, the water and the wall in a single frame. If you want something closer, Calle del Sol gives a straight-on view of the southeast facade. The garden has its own views over Old San Juan from the upper areas. Take a few wide shots first, then move in for details such as the walls and terraces. The house is very close, so you can easily try more than one angle.
text.geographic_location: Casa Blanca is in Old San Juan, on a promontory above San Juan Bay, next to the old city wall. Paseo del Morro is on the bay side of the house.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed nearby. From there the house is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade, the bay and the city wall. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and water, or if you move closer on Calle del Sol. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as windows, walls and terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Paseo del Morro (panoramic position above the path, looking back toward the southwest facade). The house's southwest facade framed against San Juan Bay, with the old city wall beside it. From here you see the southwest facade framed against San Juan Bay, with the old city wall beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the house on one third of the frame, with the bay and wall filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a close, straight-on shot of the southeast facade, try Calle del Sol instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white walls to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so they keep their detail and do not wash out against the sky. Take a panorama only if you can hold the phone steady and nobody walks through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the white walls, and a clear sky helps the bay stand out.

text.access_note: Paseo del Morro is a public path, but the house and garden are part of a museum, so check the official site before you go for what is open and any entry rules.

name: Calle Fortaleza
label: Calle Fortaleza
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plazuela La Rogativa' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plazuela de la Rogativa' (relation/3613992): middle (70 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W22229776 (Calle de la Fortaleza): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Colourful street of Old San Juan with its hanging umbrellas and balconies.

text.description:
Calle Fortaleza is a car-free cobblestone block in Old San Juan. It is best known for the colourful display hung across it overhead. The display changes with the season and with events. Visitors have described umbrellas, kites, butterflies and flags, so what you find may differ from older photos. The street runs toward La Fortaleza, the Governor's residence, so a long end-to-end shot has a clear destination at the far end. That makes it easy to photograph: the cobbles lead the eye along, and the decorations make a ceiling of colour above.

There are two good ways to shoot it. From the street itself, look up at the display, or stand at one end for a long view with the decorations overhead. For a wider setting, start on Plazuela La Rogativa, a quieter, slightly raised square near the San Juan Gate. It has a statue group and a view over the harbour and the fortress. That view shows the bay more than the street, so treat it as a companion shot rather than a picture of Calle Fortaleza. The street is about 190 m away, a short walk to the south-east.

Cruise-ship days bring large crowds, especially from late morning into the afternoon. One visitor found the street restricted by security during the day, so check access before you go.
text.geographic_location: Calle Fortaleza is in Old San Juan, running toward La Fortaleza, the Governor's residence.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. Head for Old San Juan and go to Plazuela La Rogativa, near the San Juan Gate. From there the street is about 190 m (a short walk) to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: On the street, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to look up at the display and keep both sides of the block in frame. Use the default lens (1x) for the long end-to-end view. On the plazuela, use the default lens (1x) for the statue and bay, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the fortress.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plazuela La Rogativa. A quieter elevated vantage with a statue group and a panorama that takes in the harbor and the fortress, with the street reached from below rather than framed as a street shot. From this elevated square you can photograph the statue group with the harbour and the fortress behind it. The street is to the south-east and is not framed from here, so walk down to it for the main shot, then stand at one end of the block to see it run away in both directions.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the centre of the street on the middle vertical line, so the cobbles and overhead decorations are symmetrical. For the upward shot, hold the phone level and tilt it up gently so the display fills the top of the frame. On the plazuela, put the statue in the foreground and the bay behind it. The street is a good alternative if the bay is hazy.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the display to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. If people are walking through, try a Live Photo and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Aim for earlier in the day, as cruise-ship crowds build from late morning into the afternoon. One visitor saw the street opened only briefly for an evening light show, so check access before you go.

text.access_note: Plazuela La Rogativa is a square near the San Juan Gate, but access to Calle Fortaleza may be restricted at times, so check access locally before you go.

name: Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico
label: Museo de Arte PR
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/196598864: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico' (128 m across).
notes: Large art museum in Santurce with a tropical garden.

text.description: The Museum of Art of Puerto Rico stands in Santurce, a barrio of San Juan. It is a large, formal building with a long frontage, which makes it a good subject for a phone. The outline on the map is about 128 m across, so there is plenty of building to work with. The older part dates from 1920, when it was designed by architect William H. Shimmelphening as the San Juan Municipal Hospital. It worked as a hospital until 1966 and was then used as government office space until 1975. The idea of turning the site into an art museum dates to 1995. Rather than demolish the old structure, the builders folded it into the new museum building. That mix of an older hospital building and newer additions is what you are photographing. For a phone, the simplest approach is to treat it as an architecture shot. Step back until the whole frontage fits, then take a second, closer picture of a doorway, window pattern or a section of wall. Use the gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight, as a tilted phone makes a big building look as if it is leaning. If people are walking past, wait a moment for a clearer frame. Inside, photography rules can differ from room to room, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Santurce, a barrio of San Juan, Puerto Rico.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to the Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico in Santurce, the barrio of San Juan where the museum stands. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the middle of the museum site, so walk outwards a little to see the building as a whole. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full frontage, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk out towards the edge of the site and turn back until the frontage fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them. Keep the phone level and at chest height to avoid a leaning look. For a second picture, move closer and use 2x or more to fill the frame with windows, doors or a section of wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright and the walls look washed out. Use the ultra-wide only when you have room to step back, as it can stretch the corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on a building like this and fewer harsh shadows than midday.

text.access_note: Check the museum's official site before you go for any photography rules.

name: La Perla
label: La Perla
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Norzagaray' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Norzagaray nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM N3729405285 (La Perla): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Brightly painted seaside neighbourhood under the city wall.

text.description:
La Perla is a residential community on the slope below the old city wall, running down towards the Atlantic. It photographs well because the whole neighbourhood is laid out in front of you: a row of colourful houses, the well-known basketball court and the open sea beyond. The easiest way to take it in is from Calle Norzagaray, on the walkway beside the wall above the neighbourhood. From there you see the houses and the court spread down the slope without having to go into the streets below. That suits a phone well, because one frame can hold the colours, the court and the line of the coast.

Because people live here, treat it as a view rather than a set. Guides advise photographing the murals, the coast and the views only, and not people or homes without permission. Drone flying is discouraged, and daylight visits are advised.

The walkway is a pavement beside a road, with steep sections, so stop somewhere safe before you raise your phone and keep an eye on traffic. If you are heading on to the forts, Castillo San Cristóbal gives a second angle. From there La Perla's roofs and houses sit below the city wall, with the Atlantic and the El Morro lighthouse in the distance.
text.geographic_location: La Perla sits on the coastal slope just below the old city wall of Old San Juan, between the wall and the Atlantic. Calle Norzagaray runs along the wall above it, on the way to the forts.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head to Castillo San Cristóbal and the section of Calle Norzagaray above La Perla. From there, follow the wall-side walkway until the houses and the court open out below you on the north-west side. Take care on the pavement, which has traffic and steep grades, and stay on the street above rather than going down into the neighbourhood. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the row of houses, the court and the sea in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the court or a patch of colourful houses without pointing at anyone's home. The ultra-wide (0.5x) adds more sea and sky, but keep the wall edge out of the frame's corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Norzagaray (section above La Perla, along the wall-side walkway). A row of colorful houses and the basketball court spread down the slope toward the Atlantic, seen from above the neighborhood. On the section above La Perla, along the wall-side walkway. From there you look down the slope at a row of colourful houses and the basketball court spreading towards the Atlantic, seen from above the neighbourhood.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the court or the row of houses on a lower grid line, with the sea along the upper third. Keep the wall or railing out of the foreground, or use it as a deliberate edge on one side. For a different view, Castillo San Cristóbal shows the roofs below the city wall with the lighthouse in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the houses to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. Take a few shots at different zoom levels while you are in a safe spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit in daylight, as guides advise. Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually shows the colours best.

text.access_note: Calle Norzagaray is a public street with a pavement beside the wall, but La Perla itself is a residential community, so photograph from above and check current visiting details for Castillo San Cristóbal if you plan to add it.

name: Plaza de Armas
label: Plaza de Armas
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Armas' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W487051052 (Plaza de Armas): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Old San Juan's main square with its four-season fountain.

text.description:
Plaza de Armas is a colonial square where the pastel buildings and arcades around the edge do most of the work for you. The central fountain makes a natural foreground. Stand beside it and the soft-coloured facades sit behind it like a backdrop, which is why guides often single out the fountain and the facades as the most photogenic parts of the plaza. It is also an easy stop on a walking route, so you can take your pictures without a detour.

The phone icon on the map is in the centre of the plaza, by the fountain. From here the fountain fills the foreground and the buildings and arcades frame the square around it. Guides mention four statues on the fountain representing the seasons, so check on the day before deciding what to focus on.

A second, quieter frame is the bronze salsa-composer statue. Shot close, with the town hall and colonial buildings blurred behind, it makes a good contrast to the wide view.

Early morning is calmer and the light is soft. In the evening the plaza lights come on, and a human statue often performs by the fountain, which adds interest but also people in your frame. On the first Saturday of the month there are bomba performances in the plaza, which can block your view, so allow a little patience or move a few steps to find a clear gap.
text.geographic_location: Plaza de Armas is a colonial square in San Juan, surrounded by pastel colonial buildings and arcades.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or train stop for this spot, so head for Plaza de Armas in San Juan and look for the central fountain. Once you are in the square, walk to the middle, beside the fountain. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the facades behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the arcades and buildings in the same shot. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bronze statue and for details on the facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The fountain is right beside you, with the pastel colonial buildings and arcades framing the square around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the fountain in the lower part of the frame and let the coloured facades fill the background. Turn on gridlines to keep the buildings straight. For a quieter alternative, move to the bronze salsa-composer statue and frame it close, with the town hall and colonial buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the pastel colours stay rich. For the statue, try portrait mode to soften the background. In the evening, night mode can help, but hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning for fewer people and soft light. Evening is also good once the plaza lights come on, though it is busier and a human statue often performs by the fountain.

text.access_note: This is an open public plaza, but check locally for events before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone steady, or leaning on something solid, helps night-mode shots.
Lowering exposure can help keep colours rich when the sky is bright.

name: Plaza de Colón
label: Plaza de Colón
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Colón' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W196605697 (Plaza Colón): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Square with the Columbus monument at the edge of Old San Juan.

text.description:
Plaza de Colón is a small square in San Juan, and its main subject is easy to spot: a statue of Columbus on a tall column in the middle of the plaza. Colourful colonial buildings stand around it, so the column has a bright, busy backdrop whichever way you turn. That mix of monument and colour is why visitors photograph it so often. Close by there is also an I Love SJ sign, a popular second stop for selfies.

On a phone, the simplest picture is the statue on its column with the coloured façades behind it. Stand at the base of the monument and use the default lens (1x) to take in the column and the buildings together. If you want the whole column from bottom to top, step back a little and use the gridlines to keep it upright. For a second view, move to the side of the square opposite the blue Antiguo Casino and photograph the Casino across the plaza, with the stone fort of San Cristóbal visible in the distance to the north-east.

The square is small and can get crowded with vendors and people queuing for selfies. Going early in the morning gives you a clearer view and fewer people in the frame. If someone walks into your shot, take a few pictures one after another and keep the cleanest. Check the sky before you shoot: a bright sky can make the buildings look dark unless you adjust the exposure.
text.geographic_location: Plaza de Colón is a small square in San Juan, surrounded by colourful colonial buildings. The stone fort of San Cristóbal lies to its north-east.
text.directions_text: Head for Plaza Colón in San Juan. The phone icon on the map is in the centre of the square, at the base of the Columbus monument, so there is no further walk once you are in the plaza. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue, the column and the coloured buildings together. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the square is busy and you need to fit the whole column in from close to its base. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the statue itself against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand in the centre of the square, at the base of the Columbus monument. From here the statue on its tall column is in the middle of your photo, with the colourful colonial buildings around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the column on a vertical line so it stands straight. Include some of the buildings on each side for colour. For a different view, move to the side of the square opposite the blue Antiguo Casino: the plaza is then open to the morning sun, with the Casino across from you and the fort of San Cristóbal in the distance to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the column keeps its detail. Take several shots in a row while people move through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour groups and vendors arrive.

text.access_note: This is an open public square.
claims_not_in_sources: A bright sky can make buildings look dark in a phone photo unless the exposure is lowered.
Taking several shots in a row makes it easier to get one without people walking through.

name: Dos Hermanos Bridge
label: Dos Hermanos Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Playita del Condado' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Playita del Condado' (way/60958999): edge nearest the subject (970 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/430132396: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Puente Dos Hermanos' (317 m across).
notes: Historic bridge linking Condado with Old San Juan.

text.description:
Dos Hermanos Bridge (Puente Dos Hermanos) crosses the Condado Lagoon and is a pedestrian and cycling route. It links the Condado district with the land entrance to the islet where Old San Juan stands. It was designed and built by the brothers Hernand and Sosthenes Behn and opened on 22 May 1910. The name means "Two Brothers". The Behns were also behind the Condado development, and the bridge was part of making it reachable. The bridge was rebuilt and restored, and the new bridge was inaugurated in December 2011.

It photographs well because of the water on both sides. You get the calm lagoon, the line of the bridge leading the eye along the frame, and the historic fort across the water. For a closer view, walk west along the shore to Playita del Condado, the small sandy beach at the Condado end of the bridge. From there the lagoon and the start of the bridge sit in the foreground, with the fort in the distance. It is also usually quieter than the busy walkway on the bridge itself.

Take a few frames at different zoom levels: a wide one for the whole scene, then a closer one of the fort. If you also walk onto the bridge, expect little shade, so bring a hat and water. A longer view along the bridge, with the Atlantic, the lagoon and the San Juan skyline behind it, is a good second picture.
text.geographic_location: Dos Hermanos Bridge crosses the Condado Lagoon in San Juan, joining the Condado district of Santurce with the entrance to the Old San Juan islet. Playita del Condado is the small beach at the Condado end of the bridge.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed nearby, so head for the Condado area. Walk west along the shore to reach Playita del Condado, where the bridge begins at the Condado end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the beach, lagoon and bridge into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Switch to the telephoto or zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the fort in across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (sandy beach beside the road where the bridge begins, Condado end). The lagoon and the start of the bridge in the foreground, with the historic fort visible across the water. For the classic view, walk west along the shore to Playita del Condado, the sandy beach at the Condado end of the bridge. From there the lagoon and the start of the bridge are in the foreground, and the historic fort is visible across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the bridge along a lower third line, with the lagoon below and the fort and sky above. Keep the horizon level. Use a little sand or water edge in the foreground to add depth. For a different view, walk onto the bridge for its full length with the Atlantic, the lagoon and the skyline behind, or look for the Fortín de San Jerónimo del Boquerón for the bridge seen across the lagoon mouth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or fort to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the water and sky keep their colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands for the zoomed shots. Panorama mode can also work for the sweep of the lagoon.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and is more comfortable on a walkway with little shade.

text.access_note: The beach and bridge are public places for walking and cycling, but the Fortín de San Jerónimo may have restricted access or be closed for works, so check the official site before you go.
